Socket.IO: a WebSocket Library

Why reach for a library at all instead of the raw WebSocket API — fallbacks, reconnection, and rooms, all needed here anyway.

Node and every modern browser already have a raw WebSocket API — a library isn't strictly required to open one connection and send messages across it. Socket.IO earns its place in this project for what it adds on top of that raw connection, all of which this lesson actually needs: automatic reconnection if a connection drops (a laptop lid closes, wifi blips) without the app writing that retry logic by hand; a fallback to plain HTTP requests for the rare network that blocks WebSockets outright, invisible to the code using it; and — the feature the next two slides build on — rooms, a way to label a connection so a message can be broadcast to "everyone in this group" instead of one connection at a time.

Socket.IO ships two halves: a server package (socket.io, this project's dependency) and a matching client package (socket.io-client, which the React frontend built in the following weeks will use) — both speaking the same protocol on top of a WebSocket, so a client using one can only really talk to a server using the other. On the server side, it needs a real http.Server to attach itself to — not just the Express app object — which is exactly why server.js, not app.js, is where it gets wired up next.
